result.title: Helping at the Hillview Open Day
result.objective: Learners will understand and use 'take part in' and 'in charge of' to describe participation and responsibility at work.

exercises.prompt: In s2 'Volunteers may take part in a short welcome session before visitors arrive,' what does 'take part in' mean here?

options.text: It means to participate in the welcome session.
options.explanation: It is correct because volunteers will join and participate in the session.

options.text: It means to watch the welcome session without joining it.
options.explanation: It is wrong because the phrase means active participation, not only watching.

options.text: It means to cancel the welcome session for visitors.
options.explanation: It is wrong because the sentence is about joining the session, not cancelling it.

exercises.explanation: The phrase describes participating in the welcome session.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that uses 'take part in' correctly and naturally.

options.text: Many students took part in the school clean-up day last Saturday.
options.explanation: It is correct because past tense 'took part in' is used naturally with an event.

options.text: She take part in the training workshop every Friday.
options.explanation: It is wrong because 'take' should be 'takes' to agree with 'She'.

options.text: They took part on the charity run last month.
options.explanation: It is wrong because 'on' should be 'in' in the fixed phrase 'took part in'.

exercises.explanation: Only one sentence uses the correct verb form and preposition.

exercises.prompt: In s3 'One coordinator is in charge of the welcome desk,' what does 'in charge of' mean here?

options.text: It means to visit the welcome desk as a guest.
options.explanation: It is wrong because the phrase means responsibility, not visiting as a guest.

options.text: It means to be responsible for managing the welcome desk.
options.explanation: It is correct because the coordinator is responsible for managing the desk.

options.text: It means to leave the welcome desk without help.
options.explanation: It is wrong because the phrase means looking after the desk, not leaving it.

exercises.explanation: The phrase describes responsibility for the welcome desk.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that uses 'in charge of' correctly and naturally.

options.text: She is in charge for the new project team.
options.explanation: It is wrong because 'for' should be 'of' in the fixed phrase 'in charge of'.

options.text: Mr. Lee is in charge of the evening shift at the restaurant.
options.explanation: It is correct because 'in charge of' is used naturally to show responsibility.

options.text: They are in charges of organizing the conference.
options.explanation: It is wrong because 'charges' should be 'charge' in the fixed phrase.

exercises.explanation: Only one sentence uses the correct fixed phrase and grammar.

exercises.prompt: You are an office worker writing a short message to a friend about a company sports event. Write 2–3 sentences describing what you did and inviting your friend next time. Use a form of 'take part in' in your answer.
exercises.sampleAnswer: I took part in our company football tournament last Saturday. It was fun and our team played well. You should join us next time!
selfCheck: I used a correct form of 'take part in' naturally.
My message is from an office worker to a friend about a sports event, not about the arts centre welcome session.
exercises.explanation: Compare with the model and self-assess; no automatic grade.
